coreTruths.title: The mouth is forgiving, but surgical principles still apply
coreTruths.broaderContext: Good blood supply and saliva mean the mouth heals well, but that biology is not a free pass. Sloppy technique still produces pain, infection, and delayed healing.
coreTruths.body:
## The mouth tolerates surgery, it does not reward sloppiness

The mouth heals well thanks to its rich blood supply and the protective properties of saliva, and it copes with its own commensal load better than expected [1]. That tolerance is not a licence to skip the basics: incisions, retraction, bone removal, debridement, and closure all still need to be done properly [1].

## Anatomy and pathology drive every decision

Know the anatomy and the operation makes sense. Know the pathology and the why becomes clear, including what can be sacrificed and what must be preserved [2]. That is what separates planned surgery from a hopeful attempt.

## Debridement matters as much as the cut itself

Leftover bone dust under a flap is one of the commonest causes of post-operative pain and delayed healing [3]. Cleaning the wound is part of the operation, not an afterthought. The same goes for haemostasis and gentle handling: post-operative oedema is minimised by efficient surgery far more than by ice packs or steroids [4].

citations.quote: The mouth is a remarkably forgiving environment in which to operate, because of its excellent blood supply and the properties of saliva. It is compromised less than could be expected by its teeming hordes of commensal organisms. This does not, however, constitute carte blanche for ignoring the basic principles of surgery, although these can and should be modified to suit the nature and the site of the surgery.

These are the interdependent building blocks of surgery. Know the anatomy and you can understand the operation. Know the pathology and you know why you are doing it, what can be sacrificed, and what must be preserved.

Debridement is removal from the wound of debris generated by both the pathology and the operation. It is as important as any other part of the operation. Subperiosteal bone dust is a common cause of pain and delayed wound healing.

Post-operative oedema is, to some degree, inevitable; it is minimized by gentle efficient surgery, which is more important than such measures as ice packs and peri- or post-operative steroids, although these can help.

coreTruths.title: Access plus atraumatic technique beats small flaps and brute force
coreTruths.broaderContext: Surgical extractions and dento-alveolar work fail when access is poor. Bigger flaps, controlled forces, and elevators on impacted teeth heal better than fighting through a small window.
coreTruths.body:
## Big flaps heal as well as small ones

A bigger flap that gives proper access nearly always beats a small one that forces traumatic surgery. The cost of extra periosteal stripping is more than paid back by gentler bone removal and tooth delivery [1]. Plan one clean cut at right angles through mucoperiosteum to bone, avoid splitting interdental papillae, and lift subperiosteally with a blunt instrument [2].

## Use the right instrument with the right force

Elevators are the instrument of choice for impacted teeth, used with finger pressure rather than shoulder weight [3]. Forceps work by dilating the socket, applying blades along the root, then moving the tooth in the direction its root anatomy allows: rotate conical roots, work bucco-palatally on flattened roots, rock divergent molar roots [4].

## When the tooth will not move, stop and re-plan

If a tooth refuses to budge, do not just press harder. Get an X-ray, look for diverging roots, ankylosis, or sclerotic bone, and shift to a trans-alveolar approach [5]. Pressing on regardless costs time and goodwill and risks fracturing alveolar bone or breaking the tooth.

## Bone removal needs irrigation

Drills must run with sterile irrigation. Without it, heat necrosis of bone, soft tissue damage, and a clogged bur are all on the table [6].

citations.quote: Improved access via a large flap, allowing minimally traumatic surgery, virtually always outweighs the trauma of additional periosteal stripping.

Always plan the incision mindful of local structures. One cut, at right angles, through mucoperiosteum to bone, is the aim. Blade blunts on touching bone. Do not split interdental papillae. Try to cut in the depth of the gingival sulcus. Raise the flap cleanly, working subperiosteally with a blunt instrument, moving from easily elevated areas to the more difficult.

These are used to dilate sockets to facilitate extraction or to remove dental hard tissue by themselves. These are the instruments which should always be used to remove impacted teeth. They should be used with gentle (finger pressure) forces.

The socket is dilated either using an elevator between the bone of the socket wall and the tooth or by driving the forceps blades into the socket. The blades of the forceps are applied to the buccal and palatal/lingual aspects of the tooth and pushed either along the root of the tooth or, in certain molar extractions, into the bifurcation. The tooth is then gripped in the forceps and, maintaining a consistent and quite substantial vertical force, the tooth is moved depending on its anatomy.

Don’t worry; it happens to us all. Have you got an X-ray? If not, get one and look for: bulbous or diverging roots, very long roots, ankylosis, or sclerotic bone. Do not press on regardless; it will work sometimes but shows lack of consideration and will cost you in time and goodwill in the long run. Most ‘solid’ teeth have an easily identifiable cause, e.g. diverging roots, and raising a flap and using a trans-alveolar procedure will quickly and easily remedy this.
Bone removal by drills must be accompanied by sterile irrigation to prevent heat necrosis of bone, damage to soft tissues, and clogging of the bur.

coreTruths.title: Anti-resorptive drugs change the rules of dento-alveolar surgery
coreTruths.broaderContext: Bisphosphonates, denosumab, and anti-angiogenics block the osteoclast activity that healing sockets need. Surgery on these patients is a risk-stratified decision, not a routine extraction.
coreTruths.body:
## Avoid surgery that needs bone remodelling

The core principle is simple: do not perform surgery that requires osteoclast activity for healing on a patient taking these drugs unless there is no alternative [1]. Endodontics, coronectomy, and other tooth-saving routes get pushed up the priority list because they sidestep the problem.

## Risk varies wildly with the drug and the indication

The MRONJ risk is not one number. It runs from less than 1% in a low-risk osteoporosis patient to roughly 30% in a myeloma survivor at ten years [2]. Consent has to reflect the patient sitting in the chair, not a generic average.

## If extraction is unavoidable, change the technique

When surgery cannot be avoided, the recipe is prophylactic chlorhexidine and broad-spectrum antibiotic, atraumatic extraction, alveolar septoplasty so all bone sits well below the gingival margin, and primary mucosal closure [2]. The logic is that vascularised mucosal cover stops superinfection of bone that will not remodel on its own.

## Render dentally fit before the drug starts

For patients about to start bisphosphonates, the right mindset is the same one used before head and neck radiotherapy: try to set them up so they never need a tooth out in future [3]. The balance is real and not everyone gets cleared to edentulism, but the bias is toward heroic prevention.

citations.quote: The principle is not to carry out any surgery which requires osteoclast activity for healing on someone taking these drugs.

If not, warn the patient of risks (range from <1% for low-risk drug in osteoporosis patient to 30% in a myeloma survivor at 10yrs). Use prophylactic chlorhexidine and broad-spectrum antibiotic, atraumatic extraction, and alveolar septoplasty to ensure all bone lies well below the gingival margin and close mucosa primarily. This is on the basis that vascularized mucosal coverage will prevent superinfection of bone that will not remodel.

If you are asked to render ‘dentally fit’ someone who is to start bisphosphonates, it is probably best to adopt a similar approach to those having head and neck radiotherapy—try to ensure they never need to have a tooth removed in the future.

coreTruths.title: Third molar decisions are about symptoms and pathology, not prophylaxis
coreTruths.broaderContext: Wisdom teeth attract a lot of unnecessary surgery. The current logic is to remove only those causing trouble, and to plan around the inferior dental nerve when extraction is needed.
coreTruths.body:
## Not every wisdom tooth needs to come out

Third molars that have space to erupt into function should be left to do so, and deeply impacted asymptomatic ones are usually best left alone [1]. Prophylactic removal of symptomless third molars is hard to justify [2], and preventing lower incisor crowding does not count as an indication on its own [3].

## Pericoronitis is the dominant indication

Most wisdom teeth come out for recurrent pericoronitis, unrestorable caries in the 7 or 8, resorption, cystic change, or periodontal disease distal to the 7 [3]. A tooth that has breached mucosa will almost always become infected eventually, while one fully covered by bone rarely will [4].

## Plan the path of withdrawal before picking up a bur

Assessment is angulation, depth, what the tooth is impacted against, root shape, bone density, the relationship to the ID canal, and any other pathology [5]. Then the question is which obstructions to remove and whether sectioning the tooth gives a kinder path of withdrawal [6]. The patient gets warned about pain, trismus, swelling, and the possibility of ID and lingual nerve damage before they consent [7].

## Stay buccal to protect the lingual nerve

Manipulation from the lingual aspect is now linked to unnecessary lingual nerve morbidity. Bone and tooth removal should come from the buccal side [8].

## Coronectomy when the root sits in the canal

If the roots are radiographically tangled with the ID canal, signs include darkening of the root, narrowing or diversion of the canal, interruption of the lamina dura, or a juxta-apical area, then taking the crown off and leaving the roots is a reasonable alternative [9]. Conventional surgical removal carries reported altered sensation rates of 8% temporary and 3.6% permanent [10], so the case for nerve preservation is real.

citations.quote: Not all wisdom teeth need to be removed.1 Most clinicians will follow the NICE guidance although currently the guidelines are under review. Those which have space to erupt into functional occlusion should be left to do so, and those which are deeply impacted and asymptomatic are best left alone.

Symptoms are most common in the late teens and twenties; bone is soft, spongy, and elastic in this age group, so this is the usual and most favourable time to operate. Prophylactic removal of symptomless third molars is currently hard to justify.4

Recurrent pericoronitis, unrestorable caries in 7 or 8, external or internal resorption, cystic change, or periodontal disease distally in 7. The prevention of LLS crowding on its own is not an indication, nor is vague TMJ pain.

Third molars covered by bone are very unlikely to become infected, whereas those where the crown has breached mucosa will almost inevitably do so. Infections in older, less vascular bone are more difficult to treat.

Assess angulation (vertical, mesio-angular, disto-angular, horizontal, or transverse); depth of impaction from the alveolar crest to the maximum diameter of the crown; degree of impaction (and against what); root shape; bone density; the relationship to the ID canal; and the presence of any other pathology or complicating factors.

Plan the path of withdrawal (Fig. 10.5). What impedes it? How much bone needs to be removed to provide a point of application for an elevator? How much to clear the path of withdrawal? Can this be done less traumatically by sectioning the tooth? In what direction?
Warn the patient about pain, trismus, swelling, and the possibility of damage to the ID and lingual nerves.
There is now good evidence to suggest that manipulation from the lingual aspect results in unnecessary lingual nerve morbidity. Bone and tooth removal should be from a buccal approach.

Radiographic signs of ↑ risk of nerve damage include: Proximity to nerve canal. Narrowing or diversion of canal. Darkening of root/interrupting white lines of canal. Interruption of lamina dura. Juxta-apical area.

Coronectomy compares favourably to surgical removal of lower wisdom teeth in terms of altered sensation: reported rates for conventional surgical removal are 8% temporary, and 3.6% permanent (personal rates vary).

coreTruths.title: Dento-facial infections are surgical, not pharmacological problems
coreTruths.broaderContext: Tooth-borne infection rarely settles on antibiotics alone. The job is drainage and source control, with the airway as the immediate priority when swelling spreads.
coreTruths.body:
## Antibiotics do not finish the job

Infection associated with teeth is rarely, if ever, treated definitively by antibiotics and analgesics [1]. Drainage and removal of the source, whether root canal, extraction, or incision of a fluctuant abscess, is the actual treatment [2]. An abscess is a collection of pus relatively isolated from the circulation, which is exactly why antibiotics on their own do not reach it [3].

## Airway first, every time

Anyone struggling to swallow their own saliva needs admission immediately because the airway is at risk [4]. People die from these infections, particularly when they spread to the fascial spaces of the neck, mediastinum, or cavernous sinus [5]. Ludwig's angina, with bilateral submandibular and sublingual swelling and a board-hard floor of mouth, is the textbook example and an urgent admission [6].

## Cellulitis behaves differently from abscess

Cellulitis is intra- and intercellular oedema. It has a good blood supply and responds to high-dose antibiotics [7]. Most head and neck infections are a mix of the two, which is why drainage and antibiotics work together rather than as alternatives [8].

## Best-guess antibiotics target anaerobes plus streps

Culture of dento-facial infections shows commensals dominated by anaerobes, mostly Bacteroides and streptococci, usually penicillin sensitive, with Bacteroides nearly always sensitive to metronidazole [9]. Cover both pathogen groups; do not lean on metronidazole alone in established infection [9]. Standard regimens are amoxicillin 500mg tds or metronidazole 400mg tds for 5 to 7 days [2].

citations.quote: Infection associated with teeth is rarely, if ever, treated definitively by antibiotics and analgesics.

Drainage of pus either via the root canal, by incision of any fluctuant abscess, or by extraction under LA or GA. Palatal or buccal abscesses can be drained quite simply under LA by infiltrating a small amount of LA between the abscess cavity and the overlying mucosa, then incising the abscess. Explore using blunt closed forceps and keep patent either by excising an ellipse of tissue or inserting and suturing a small rubber drain; this is particularly important in the palate. Cover the procedure with ‘best guess’ antibiotics such as amoxicillin 500mg tds PO for 5–7 days, or metronidazole 400mg tds PO for 5–7 days, or both. For severe infections, in-patient management with EO drainage may be needed.

An abscess is a collection of pus (white cells, inflammatory exudates, tissue fluid, and bacteria), it is relatively isolated from the circulation (and hence antibiotics). Treatment is drainage which continues until all pus is gone.
Ask about the airway. Anyone having difficulty swallowing their own saliva should be admitted immediately as the airway is at risk. People can die from these infections.

The vast majority of infections in this area requiring surgical Rx are bacterial, usually arising from necrotic pulps, periodontal pockets, or pericoronitis. They can be life-threatening if allowed to progress, e.g. to the fascial spaces of the neck, mediastinum, or the cavernous sinus, or as a focus for infective endocarditis.

This is a combination of abscess and cellulitis affecting both submandibular and sublingual spaces bilaterally. The floor of the mouth is raised and the tongue pushed up and back. The floor of mouth, tongue, and soft tissues of the neck are board hard. The patient is systemically unwell and often cannot swallow their own saliva. The airway is seriously at risk and this is an urgent case for admission.

This is intra- and intercellular oedema generated by inflammatory exudates. The overlying surface is red and hot and it allows the rapid migration of bacteria to surrounding areas (Fig. 10.12). It has a good blood supply and high-dose antibiotics are the Rx of choice.
These are usually a combination of both.

Culture of dento-facial infections usually produces several commensal organisms, of which anaerobes are the most important. The predominant species, Bacteroides species (anaerobe) and streptococci (aerobe and anaerobe), are usually sensitive to the penicillins. Resistance is reported rarely. Bacteroides species are nearly always sensitive to metronidazole. Remember the aerobic pathogens in established infection (don’t just rely on metronidazole), and Haemophilus and Staphylococcus aureus near the antrum, and Streptococcus milleri is a particularly virulent pathogen present in aggressive potentially life-threatening infections.

coreTruths.title: Post-extraction bleeding has three sources and a stepwise management
coreTruths.broaderContext: Most bleeding after extractions is anxiety-amplified gingival or socket bone bleeding, not haemorrhage. Identifying the source is what makes the management work.
coreTruths.body:
## Three timings, three meanings

Post-operative bleeding is classed as immediate, reactionary, and secondary [1]. Immediate means haemostasis was never achieved on the table. Reactionary occurs within 48 hours as BP rises reopen small vessels [2]. Secondary appears around seven days out, usually from infection destroying the clot or ulcerating local vessels [3].

## The source dictates the treatment

Bleeding comes from one or more of three places: gingival capillaries, vessels in socket bone, or a large vessel under a flap or in bone [3]. The first two are by far the most common. Squeezing the gingivae against the socket walls between finger and thumb is the test: if bleeding stops, it is gingival, and a tight interrupted or mattress suture under LA will close it [4]. If it carries on, it is bone, and a pack is needed [4].

## Manage the patient before chasing the vessel

Reassure first. These patients are seldom shocked, but are usually anxious, nauseated by the taste and smell of blood, and made worse by blood in the stomach [3]. Take a drug history (anticoagulants), wear apron and gloves because they often vomit, get them into a lit room with suction, clean the face, and find the source [4].

## Pack with thought

If the bleed comes from socket depths, clot may need clearing and replacing with a pack or resorbable mesh, with tranexamic acid or adrenaline soaked in [4]. Removing clot and packing delays healing and risks infection, so use BIPP or Whitehead's varnish if packing is necessary [4]. Failure of these measures plus pressure pack means a hospital bed and haematological work-up [4].

citations.quote: Classically, post-operative bleeding is described as immediate (1°), reactionary, and 2°.
Occurs within 48h of surgery and is due to both general and local rises in BP opening up small divided vessels which were not bleeding at completion of surgery.

Occurs ~7 days post-operatively and is usually due to infection destroying the clot or ulcerating local vessels. In practice, bleeding following removal of teeth is common and usually simple to diagnose. The patients are seldom shocked or hypotensive but are often very anxious and nauseated by the taste, smell, and sight of blood, and by blood in the stomach, which is irritant. Bleeding usually comes from one or all of three sources: (i) gingival capillaries; (ii) vessels in the bone of the socket; and (iii) a large vessel under a flap or in bone, such as the inferior alveolar artery. The first two are by far the more common.

Give LA if needed, and have assistance with suction. If a flap is involved, remove old sutures, evacuate clot, identify bleeding point, and place a tight suture around it. Bleeding should be much d; if not, repeat until it is, then close wound and have the patient bite on a swab for at least 15min. If it is a gingival bleed, a tight interrupted or mattress suture will compress the capillaries, again followed by a swab to bite on. If bleeding is from the depths of the socket, the clot may need to be removed and replaced by a pack or supported by a resorbable mesh (oxidized cellulose) &/or agents such as tranexamic acid, adrenaline, or epsilon aminocaproic acid soaked into the mesh. If removing clot and packing the socket, remember this will delay healing and predispose to infection, so use bismuth iodoform paraffin paste (BIPP) or Whitehead’s varnish packs. If all else fails, use all the earlier mentioned measures plus a pressure pack, analgesia, an antiemetic, and a night in a hospital bed. Patients requiring this degree of Rx should be investigated haematologically and for liver disease.

coreTruths.title: Biopsy is the answer when clinical diagnosis is uncertain
coreTruths.broaderContext: Many oral lesions look benign and are not. The threshold for histopathology is low because the cost of guessing wrong is delayed cancer diagnosis.
coreTruths.body:
## When in doubt, biopsy

Any soft tissue lesion the eye cannot diagnose with confidence is a candidate for biopsy. All red lesions of oral mucosa and most white patches should be biopsied [1]. The rule of thumb is straightforward: if the question "should I biopsy this?" comes up, the answer is yes, because the surprises tend to be the unpleasant ones [1].

## Excise everything sent for examination

Nearly everything worth excising is worth histological review, so all excised specimens go to the lab [1]. Excisional biopsy makes sense for very small lesions where the whole thing can come out with a margin [2]. For larger or suspicious lesions, an incisional biopsy with an ellipse of lesion plus surrounding normal tissue is the standard [2].

## Refer suspected malignancy before biopsying it

Incisional biopsy carries a theoretical risk of shedding malignant cells into the circulation [3]. The bigger practical issue is that most consultants have a preferred approach and want to integrate diagnosis with counselling. So when oral malignancy is on the cards, the move is to refer before cutting [3].

## Handle the specimen properly

Small specimens go on paper, large ones get pinned to a cork board to prevent shrinkage artefact [4]. Standard preservative is 10% formalin, but some tests need fresh tissue, so check before sending [4]. A diagram on the form, and a clinical note that says what is suspected, helps the pathologist do their job [5].

citations.quote: Nearly everything that is worth excising is worth histological review, and so all excised specimens should be examined histopathologically. Any soft tissue lesion not amenable to accurate clinical ∆ (by a reasonably trained eye) should be biopsied. All red lesions of oral mucosa and most white patches should be biopsied. If you think ‘Should I biopsy this?’ then do it; you will always get some unpleasant surprises.

Biopsies may be incisional or excisional. Examples of incisional biopsies are fine-needle aspirate (really cytology), punch biopsy, trephines, and ‘true-cut’ needle biopsy. The commonest technique by far, however, is to excise an ellipse of tissue that includes a portion of the lesion and surrounding normal tissue. Excisional biopsy provides after the fact information on the excised sample (reserve for very small lesions).

Incisional biopsy carries a (theoretical) risk of shedding malignant cells into the circulation. The alternative is to subject a patient to mutilating surgery before definitive ∆. If you suspect an oral malignancy, refer before biopsy because most consultants have a preferred approach. This also allows integrated ∆ and counselling.

Specimens are best laid out on paper if small or pinned out on a cork board if large. This allows orientation and ↓ shrinkage artefact, which can be considerable. Usual preservative is 10% formalin; ask if you are not sure, as some specimens are needed fresh. Consider a specimen for culture as well (e.g. lymph node biopsy). Make a diagram of the specimen on the pathology form to accompany the clinical details. A photograph of the operative site can help.
Tell the pathologist what you are thinking!

coreTruths.title: Jaw cysts: enucleate, close primarily, and always send for histology
coreTruths.broaderContext: Most jaw cysts are odontogenic and benign, but a small fraction (especially keratocysts) recur or hide more aggressive lesions. The technique and the histology together protect the patient.
coreTruths.body:
## Enucleation with primary closure is the default

For most jaw cysts, the treatment is to remove the cyst lining from the bony walls and reposition the access flap, dealing with any related dental pathology in the same sitting (often by apicectomy) [1]. Marsupialisation is reserved for letting a tooth erupt through a cyst or where enucleation is contraindicated, but healing is slower and a cavity persists [2].

## Always send the lining

Every cyst lining goes for histopathology, no exceptions [3]. The lining is what tells the difference between a radicular cyst, a dentigerous cyst, an odontogenic keratocyst, or worse.

## Keratocysts deserve respect

Odontogenic keratocysts are lined by parakeratinised epithelium with outpouching walls and daughter cysts that explain their tendency to recur [4]. Their multiloculated X-ray appearance can be confused with ameloblastoma. Treatment is careful enucleation, often with cryotherapy or Carnoy's solution or aggressive curettage [4]. Excision is reserved for the recurrent ones [4].

## Inflammatory cysts come from necrotic pulps

Radicular cysts are very common. The stimulus is necrotic pulp and the epithelium comes from cell rests of Malassez. The treatment combines enucleation with either endodontics or extraction of the source tooth [5]. Treating the cyst without dealing with the cause is half the job.

## Diagnosis starts with X-ray and vitality testing

Most cysts turn up as asymptomatic radiolucencies or painless buccal swellings; infected ones present with pain, swelling, and discharge [6]. Vitality test the associated teeth, get a DPT and a periapical, and consider aspiration where it might help differentiate the lesion [6].

citations.quote: Enucleation with 1° closure is commonest and generally the Rx of choice. It consists of removing the cyst lining from the bony walls of the cavity and repositioning the access flap. Any relevant dental pathology is treated at the same time, e.g. by apicectomy.

Marsupialization. This is the opening of the cyst to allow continuity with the oral mucosa; healing is slower than with enucleation and a cavity persists for some time. It is useful to allow tooth eruption through the cyst or where enucleation is C/I.
Always submit cyst lining for histopathology.

Keratocystic odontogenic tumour (KCOT) is an odontogenic cyst that can be rapidly growing. In 2005 the WHO reclassified the lesions as KCOT due to their propensity to reoccur and invade local tissues. This term was not used commonly and in 2017 the name reverted to odontogenic keratocyst. They are lined by parakeratinized epithelium derived from the remnants of the dental lamina and are thought to replace a missing tooth. They have a fluid filling with a protein content <4g/dL. Aspiration of samples for biochemistry and cytology for parakeratinized squames can be helpful. It is important to identify these cysts, as outpouching walls and ‘daughter’ or ‘satellite’ cysts make them more liable to recur. Their multiloculated appearance on X-ray may confuse them with an ameloblastoma. Rx: careful enucleation, &/or cryotherapy &/or Carnoy’s solution, or aggressive curettage of the cavity. Rarely, excision is needed if recurrent.

These are very common, and may also be called radicular cysts. Described as apical or lateral depending on position in relation to tooth root, or residual if left behind after tooth extraction. Necrotic pulp is the stimulus, and the epithelium comes from cell rests of Malassez. Rx: enucleation plus endodontics or extraction.

Many are detected as asymptomatic radiolucencies on X-ray; others present as painless swellings, almost always of the buccal cortex. Infected cysts present with pain, swelling, and discharge. Vitality test associated teeth. Take a DPT and a periapical film when possible to screen for size and coexisting pathology. Transillumination rarely helps, but aspiration is sometimes useful and can help distinguish some lesions. Rarely, cysts may present with a pathological #, especially of the mandible.
